name: URO-Bench
ability_definition: The ability to communicate information and ideas in speaking so others will understand.

task_realism.reasoning: The model produces its own spoken content: it answers questions, explains, and holds multi-turn conversations across many test sets. That is closer to real oral expression than reading given text aloud. However, many subsets are text QA, math or reasoning datasets converted to speech. They do not resemble workplace speaking tasks such as briefing a colleague, explaining a procedure to a customer, or presenting to a group.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Scoring relies on automatic proxies: ASR transcription followed by an LLM judge, plus UTMOS and WER. No human listener checks whether they actually understood. Inputs are largely synthesized or clean speech, with no real audience, stakes, interruptions or noisy settings. Responses are scored in isolation rather than by communicative outcome.

construct_coverage.reasoning: It covers two core parts of the ability: content correctness and coherence (judged on the transcript) and basic intelligibility and audio quality (WER and UTMOS). It also includes multilingual and multi-turn conversation. It largely misses adapting to the listener, structuring longer explanations, and the prosody and emphasis that aid comprehension. It also misses whether a specific audience grasps the ideas.

format_match.reasoning: Speech in and speech out is the natural format for oral expression, and outputs are free-form spoken answers rather than forced choices. The format is still bounded by the benchmark: mostly short, single-response or brief multi-turn exchanges. These differ from extended, audience-directed workplace speech.

transferability_reasoning: URO-Bench measures the right modality: the system generates its own spoken responses, which are checked for correctness and intelligibility. That makes it a reasonable proxy for oral expression. Transfer is limited because many tasks are text benchmarks repurposed for speech, and evaluation depends on ASR and LLM-judge stand-ins rather than real listeners. It also underweights audience adaptation and extended explanatory speech typical of the workplace.
